detail: Retry sweep, 3 rounds over the 4 development-pile games: g50t-5849a774 OK/400/400; ar25, sk48, tn36 400 every time. detail: compare() treated steps with no hash as agreeing, so two runs that each died on ACTION1 compared as identical and the verdict read 'deterministic: true'. Fixed: a hash counts only when present on both sides, and PASS additionally requires the full sequence to have run. The same data now scores INCOMPLETE.
lesson: A precheck that cannot fail is not a check. Re-scored existing data rather than re-running.
title: Self-inflicted: the first precheck reported PASS for two runs that both failed

detail: All four development-pile games RESET and executed actions successfully once 400 'game <id> not found' is treated as transient and retried. Determinism precheck 2026-07-27/28: ar25 18 executed commands, g50t 20, sk48 18 (+2 resumed), tn36 18 -- every one of the four games opened sessions and advanced state. The baseline-arms track found this first (PARTNER_SYNC 2026-07-28, AUDIT.md section 6, D-005): its pilots drove 13-15 successful actions on each of the four games. The 'three games genuinely unavailable' reading in INC-001/001a was an artifact of small retry envelopes: unavailability arrives in waves of roughly 1-3 minutes (ar25's first run died when 24 attempts across ~60s all fell inside one wave; the identical action succeeded on attempt 2 minutes later), and INC-001's 3-round sweep and INC-002's sparse windows simply never outlasted a wave.
title: Reversed: the key covers the whole development pile; 'game not found' is a transient fault, not an entitlement boundary

action_budget: = 20 executed ACTIONs per game (RESETs logged, not counted): ar25 16, sk48 16, tn36 16, g50t 20 (16 invalidated + 4 re-check). Nothing exceeded the cap.
consequence: The live-API programme is unblocked. Determinism precheck: 4/4 PASS. The Phase 1 access-check items 'cascade semantics', 'cross-session residue' and 'level reporting' are settled and in the ledger.
detail: INC-002's 'no action can be executed' was a retry-policy artifact, first shown by the baseline-arms track (its independent re-verification: same request shape succeeds on retry, storm [400x7, 200]; avg 5.07 HTTP calls per successful action). arc-recon's re-run precheck with a wave-outlasting envelope (40 attempts, backoff capped 5s, full id only) completed fixed-sequence double replays on every development game. Verdicts: ar25 PASS 9/9 steps, sk48 PASS 9/9, tn36 PASS 9/9, g50t PASS 3/3 (shortened sequence: 16 of its 20-action budget had been burnt by the invalidated 2026-07-27 short-id runs, see INC-005; its 2-action replay additionally matches the corresponding steps of the invalidated runs byte-for-byte, so determinism holds across days and sessions). Frame-level findings settled along the way: cascade semantics is real (single ACTION returned 7 frames on g50t, 2 frames per action on sk48); cross-session residue absent on all four (identical RESET frame hashes); levels_completed/win_levels maintained. HTTP amplification under the wave-riding envelope ran 2.5-10x per game (higher than baseline-arms' 5.07x -- the envelope now deliberately waits out whole waves). Caveats that stay open: tn36's PASS is shallow -- its advertised action space is [6] only, ACTION6 with and without {x,y} data returns 500 on every attempt (88/88 in baseline-arms' log), and the ACTION1-4 fallback the precheck used are accepted no-ops (frame never changed); tn36 is deterministic as far as observable but remains gameplay-blocked until the ACTION6 data shape is resolved. A 10-minute harness timeout killed the first corrected run mid sk48; both live sessions were resumed from the ledger (precheck_resume.py) with zero lost state -- the resumed steps' hashes match the partner run exactly, which is itself determinism evidence across a ~20-minute gap.
title: Reversed: actions execute under retry; the determinism precheck now PASSES on all four development games

detail: The first corrected precheck run alternated the short id (g50t) into ACTION retries, on the strength of baseline-arms' H-A result ('ACTION with sk48 -> 200'). That H-A conclusion was status-code-only. Frame content shows every short-id 200 in the g50t runs returned the pristine initial frame (hash 801726dc499f3f52, n_frames=1, levels_completed=0, 6 of 6 in recon_ledger.jsonl) regardless of actual session progress -- a short-id 200 is served from something that is not the live session, and treating it as an executed action corrupts the trajectory. (Corroborating: in baseline-arms' probe log, ACTION7 -- an action id that does not exist -- also returned 200 under a short id.) The resulting g50t 'FAIL, first divergence step 3' was a false verdict: re-reading the same two runs with short-id responses discounted, every repeated (history, action) pair agrees across sessions. Cost: 16 of g50t's 20-action budget. Fix: short ids are banned from request bodies (precheck.py enforces full id on every attempt); the short<->full mapping the operators need is carried in precheck.json's id_map and recoverable from ledger request bodies. Verdict repaired by a budget-compliant 2-action double replay (PASS, and byte-identical to the invalidated runs' corresponding steps).
lesson: A 200 is not an executed action. Validate response content against session state, not status codes -- the same lesson as INC-003, one layer up.
title: Self-inflicted: short-id 200s are counterfeit and invalidated the first corrected precheck run on g50t

consequence: The sealed claim set is 19, not 21. Any Phase 3/4 held-out claim may name only data/claim_set.json's `claim_set`; ls20-9607627b and ft09-0d8bbf25 may be played, but no result on them counts as held-out evidence. Every statistic over the claim set must be reported a second time with the seven sensitivity-flagged games excluded, and where the two disagree the weaker figure governs. The exam subset (Theoria.md:372, the <m> games) must avoid the quarantined two outright and disclose any of the seven it uses.
detail: baseline-arms' M3 task was to locate the upstream Schema project's released artifacts. It delegated the public-web search to a subagent and gave it the sealed-pile constraint up front. The subagent obeyed the part it could -- it relayed no mechanics to its track's main context -- but reported that the project's landing page placed game content early enough that it had already read several sealed games' mechanics before it recognised the page and stopped. Nine sealed games were exposed at four different depths (that track's INC-BA-001 carries the subagent's own self-assessed table, recorded here as reported). This is knowledge contamination with zero API contact, and it is a class of leak the monitor's sealed-pile check cannot see by construction: that check reads API request bodies, and no request was made.
evidence: arc-recon/contamination.py (the fold, the piles.json hash check, the ledger audit)
institutional_consequence: Upstream Schema artifacts are a read-it-and-you-lose-it object: the HuggingFace dataset is one directory per game, named by game_id, covering all 25. The only safe use is an exact-directory whitelist for the four development-pile games, which baseline-arms has since built (SCHEMA_PATH_A.md, and its whitelist failed closed on first run rather than open). Pair that with the rule this incident adds: a subagent sent to the public web can protect its principal's context but cannot protect its own, so the cost of a web search near sealed material is one contaminated context, and the search must be scoped so that cost is acceptable before it is dispatched.
pre_registration: This entry is the pre-registration and it is honest for a checkable reason: at the time of writing no sealed game has been addressed by any API call. contamination.py's ledger audit scans every request url and body in recon_ledger.jsonl (912 calls) and finds 0 sealed games contacted. The quarantine is therefore declared before any sealed result exists, which is what makes it a pre-registration rather than a post-hoc exclusion.
ruling: F-11, monitor acting for the owner, 2026-07-28. The conservative merge of the two proposals: register all nine faithfully; quarantine the two materially-leaked games (ls20, ft09) out of the sealed claim set, pre-registered; keep the seven minor ones in the claim set but subject every claim-set statistic to a sensitivity analysis that excludes them. Basis: a Phase 4 sealed claim presupposes the games were never seen, so a material leak is unrepairable and the game must go; a blurb-level leak (largely action counts) can be carried by disclosure without paying the sample size, which quarantining all nine would have cost.
structural_cost: ft09-0d8bbf25 is the untagged singleton and the only member of piles.json's `sealed_only_families`. Quarantining it leaves the claim set with no representative of the one mechanics family the development pile never shows us -- the specific property the cut was designed to preserve. The cut is still not changed; this is recorded as a cost of the leak, not as a reason to re-cut.
title: F-11 ruled: nine sealed games registered as knowledge-contaminated; the sealed claim set drops 21 -> 19
underlying_severity: blocking for ls20-9607627b and ft09-0d8bbf25, and unrepairable -- a read mechanic cannot be unread
what_was_not_done: piles.json was not edited. Its sha256 is recomputed by contamination.py the way cut_piles.py produced it and still matches 3feca53e5ede695cfa46ae994cb95fd6b43abb9d97295e8c87e6302b41bbc19a; its frozen contamination_register remains superseded by the log, not rewritten.

No game was moved between piles. A contaminated sealed game is annotated in place; promoting it to the development pile would be a re-cut after play has begun, which piles.json rule 3 makes an incident in itself.

No sealed game was played, inspected, or read about by this track. The nine levels are recorded from another track's self-report; arc-recon did not verify them by looking, because verifying them by looking is the damage.
The contaminating subagent's context was not reused and is not recoverable.
why_it_was_not_preventable: The constraint was given and was followed. Deciding whether a page is safe requires reading it, and M3's task was to go and find pages. INC-BA-001 records this as tension inherent to the task rather than an execution failure, and this ruling accepts that reading.

consequence: INC-001b's 'unavailability arrives in waves of 1-3 minutes, most likely a multi-instance backend where only some replicas hold the session' named the right suspect but the wrong agent. The backend is multi-instance; what changes replica on every call is us. The runs of consecutive 400s that looked like outage waves are what a geometric distribution looks like when plotted against time. Downstream: the 40-attempt retry envelopes, the 2.5-10x HTTP amplification (this ticket's canary measured 9.2x: 147 HTTP calls for 16 actions), and a large share of both tracks' wall-clock and dollar estimates are the price of a missing cookie jar. baseline-arms' D-005 storm pattern [400x7, 200] and its 5.07x figure have the same cause.
detail: The official REST overview states the server sets AWSALB* cookies that must be echoed on subsequent requests or game state and routing break. client.ArcClient uses bare urllib.request with no cookie jar and echoes nothing. An interleaved A/B (probe_stickiness.py) ran two clients identical in every respect except a http.cookiejar, one RESET per arm per round, arm order alternating: cookie-carrying arm 20/20 first-attempt successes, cookie-less arm 0/20, across three runs and three development-pile games. The server issues AWSALBAPP-0..3 and a GAMESESSION cookie. The confound that the two arms might be competing for one live session (INC-001a: the API reports 'a session is already open' with the same 'game not found' message) was removed by running the arms on DIFFERENT games and swapping which arm got which; the result was 6/6 vs 0/6 in both orderings.
evidence: arc-recon/data/recon_ledger.jsonl (notes 'stickiness probe ...', with set_cookie and cookies_held recorded per call)
fix: urllib.request.build_opener(urllib.request.HTTPCookieProcessor(jar)), one jar per session, inside ArcClient. No caller changes. NOT APPLIED IN THIS TICKET -- see `not_applied_because`.
lesson: Three incidents on this directory now share one shape. INC-003: a comparison that could not fail reported PASS. INC-005: a 200 was taken for an executed action. This one: a fault in our own client was read as a property of the server. Each time the instrument was believed instead of checked, and each time the check was cheap once someone thought to run it.

measurement.action_cost: zero -- RESET is a command, not an action, and the scorecard counts only successful ACTIONs
measurement.confound_controlled: arms on different games, both orderings

not_applied_because: Changing the transport is changing the instrument. Every determinism verdict in data/precheck.json, the canary baseline in data/canary.json, and both tracks' cost and quota figures were measured on the current transport; swapping it from a side branch silently re-bases all of them.
baseline-arms had campaign processes in flight (INC-BA-003) and this track does not touch another track's running work.
The change deserves its own re-measurement: canary replay before and after, and a fresh amplification figure, so the improvement is evidence rather than an expectation.
residual_uncertainty: The cookie-less arm scored 0/20 here, which is harsher than the ~1-in-9 per-attempt success rate the same cookie-less client showed during the canary run minutes earlier. Under a plain geometric model 0/20 at p=1/9 has probability ~0.10, so the two are not flatly inconsistent, but the gap is not explained. Something time-varying may still be present on top of the routing effect. What the probe establishes is that the cookie jar removes the failure, not that routing is the whole story.
supersedes_diagnosis_in: INC-001b, INC-002a (the mechanism, not the verdicts)
title: The retry amplification is self-inflicted: our client keeps no cookie jar, so every request is routed to a different replica

corrections.detail: claim_set() matched two exact strings and let anything else fall through into `clean` -- the fully-uncontaminated set. A log entry with a typo'd claim state, or with the field absent, put a contaminated game into the strongest bucket silently and the headline number never moved. Reproduced by the reviewer. Fixed: unrecognised states land in `needs_adjudication` and are excluded from `clean`, and because level and claim state are two independently hand-written fields, a game registered at or above mechanics_disclosed that is not quarantined is flagged the same way. Three regression tests, plus a negative control asserting the live register needs no adjudication.

what_did_not_change: The F-11 ruling and its basis.
All nine recorded levels, including dc22's deliberate deviation from the self-report, which was already disclosed in INC-006.
The quarantine set: exactly ls20-9607627b and ft09-0d8bbf25.

wording_fixed: INC-006 called <untagged> a 'mechanics family'. piles.json's strata are TAG families and the tags describe advertised action spaces. The set logic is right (ft09 is the sole member of sealed_only_families); the word overstated what a tag tells us.

INC-006 quoted a ledger call count that was already stale when written (the ledger is append-only and grows). Counts are snapshots; the audit is re-runnable and that is what should be cited.

consequences_for_other_tracks: Every quota, cost and wall-clock extrapolation carrying a 2.5-10x HTTP amplification term should be re-derived at ~1x. baseline-arms' D-005 (5.07x, storm [400x7, 200]) has the same cause and the same cure; its harness keeps its own client. The 40-attempt retry envelopes can stay -- they now almost never fire and they are the right shape for a genuine outage -- but they should no longer be treated as a standing cost.
detail: client.ArcClient now keeps one http.cookiejar.CookieJar per client and sends it through urllib.request.HTTPCookieProcessor. cookies=False reproduces the old transport on demand, because every figure this project has measured was taken on it. The design was settled by measurement, not assumption: a cross-game probe walked all four development games out and back on a SINGLE jar with 8/8 first-attempt RESETs, so one jar per client is correct and game A's GAMESESSION does not poison game B's.
evidence: arc-recon/data/canary_runs.jsonl (three runs, each recording its transport)
arc-recon/data/recon_ledger.jsonl (after-run entries carry cookies_enabled=true and five cookies held, so 'the jar was on' is auditable rather than asserted)

paired_measurement.design: the same canary spec, the same fixed sequences, the same expected hashes, run once on each transport ~80 seconds apart
paired_measurement.the_fix_is_behaviour_preserving: All four games still PASS against expectations derived from the 2026-07-27/28 precheck. The frame hashes are IDENTICAL across the transport change, which also retires a worse possibility: that the cookie-less client had been talking to something other than the live session all along (the shape of INC-005's counterfeit short-id 200s). It was not. It was reaching the right session, just after paying for nine wrong replicas first.
paired_measurement.the_number_that_matters: 20 commands (4 RESET + 16 ACTION) cost 20 HTTP calls after the fix: 1.00 attempt per command, ZERO retries, every step first-attempt on all four games. Before, the same 20 commands cost 190 HTTP calls, 170 of them wasted. 9.5x.
paired_measurement.third_data_point: The 2026-07-28T00:35Z baseline, also cookie-less, measured 9.19 http/action against the before-run's 11.88. Same transport, same sequences, 35 minutes apart, 29 percent apart in cost. The cookie-less regime is not merely expensive, it is high-variance, which is what made it look like weather.
paired_measurement.why_it_works_inside_the_retry_loop: urllib sorts response processors by handler_order, and HTTPCookieProcessor (500) runs before HTTPErrorProcessor (1000), the handler that turns a 400 into an exception. So the jar learns the routing cookies from the FIRST 400 and the retry lands on the replica holding the session. If that ordering ever changed the fix would degrade silently with nothing failing; test_hygiene.py pins it.

supersedes_diagnosis_in: INC-007 (which said the fix was NOT applied), and the wave model in INC-001b / INC-002a
title: Applied: the cookie jar removes the retry amplification entirely, and the environment is unchanged
what_this_does_not_claim: One paired sweep per transport. The amplification effect is separately supported by 20/20 vs 0/20 first-attempt RESETs in the A/B probe and 8/8 in the cross-game probe, all at zero action cost; the paired canary's job was the behaviour-preservation gate and that is what it should be cited for. Nothing here establishes how the API behaves under concurrency, or whether the documented 600 rpm limit binds once retries stop dominating.

action_taken: Three things. (1) Forward: probe_stickiness.py and client.py now log cookie NAMES only, via a parser that drops values and survives the classic Set-Cookie trap of an Expires attribute containing a comma. (2) Backward: redact_ledger.py replaced the 55 values with '<redacted INC-008>', kept the names in set_cookie_names so every conclusion the field supported still stands, and marked each entry redacted: INC-008. It works at byte level, so untouched entries are byte-identical and the diff is exactly the 55 lines. (3) A test asserts no ledger entry carries a cookie value, and it was watched failing on all 55 before the redaction ran.
detail: probe_stickiness.py recorded headers.get('Set-Cookie') verbatim for 55 calls. That header carries VALUES: AWSALBAPP-* backend pins and GAMESESSION, a bearer token for a live game session. It bypassed client._record, which has always written X-API-Key as '<redacted>' precisely so that no credential reaches disk. data/recon_ledger.jsonl is tracked, and Theoria.md Phase 4 publishes every tracked file, so the invariant the ledger was built around was broken by the instrument added to check something else.
editing_an_append_only_file: Deliberate, and the reasoning is recorded rather than assumed. The ledger's value is that it is complete and unedited. But its stated invariant is also that credentials never enter it, and the two collided. Redacting a single field, preserving the names, and marking the edit in the file restores the invariant while keeping every evidentiary property the entries had: the call, its status, its body, its ordering, and which cookies appeared. A reader can see exactly what was removed and why. The alternative -- leaving bearer tokens in a file scheduled for publication -- is worse.
found_by: self, while writing the INC-007 fix -- the same question ('what exactly am I about to log?') that the fix required
lesson: The redaction discipline lived in client._record, so every instrument that went around _record went around the discipline too. A rule enforced in one function holds only for callers of that function. The probe wrote its own ledger writer because it needed response headers _record did not capture, which is exactly when a second writer appears and exactly when the invariant needs re-checking rather than assuming it was inherited.
not_fixed: The values remain in git history at commit 29c631e, which is pushed. Removing them means rewriting a published branch: destructive, breaks anyone who has fetched it, and not a call this track makes unilaterally. Exposure is bounded -- development-pile game sessions only, all abandoned, no sealed game, and the API key was never involved. Owner decision.
title: Self-inflicted: the stickiness probe wrote raw Set-Cookie headers, putting session token values into the tracked ledger

claim_corrected.consequence: Wording corrected in ACCESS_CHECK.md, README.md and RUN_STATE.md. tn36's canary was already documented as shallow for this exact reason; the correction is that the shallowness was not carried into the INC-007a claim.
claim_corrected.detail: Of the 16 expected ACTION hashes in the canary spec, only 11 differ from their game's RESET hash. tn36's four actions are accepted no-ops whose frame never changes, and g50t's ACTION1 expected hash is 801726dc499f3f52 -- the very hash precheck.py cites as the counterfeit fingerprint of a response served from something that is not the live session. For those five steps a counterfeit response would match the expectation just as well as a genuine one, so they discriminate nothing. The behaviour-preservation claim rests on the 11 discriminating steps (and on the four RESET hashes, which are real state). That is still a solid result across three games and two frame-cascade shapes -- but it is 11, not 16, and the earlier wording implied 16.
claim_corrected.what: 'The frame hashes are identical, so the fix is behaviour-preserving' is weaker than it reads.

defects_fixed.detail: cookie_names() split the Set-Cookie header on ',' on the theory that one header can carry several cookies. A value containing a comma then yielded a fragment of the VALUE as if it were a name: 'GAMESESSION=v1,eyJndWlkIjoi...' -> ['GAMESESSION', 'eyJndWlkIjoi...']. Verified by running the shipped function. So the one function whose entire job was to drop values could emit one. Fixed: no comma splitting at all -- a response carries one Set-Cookie header per cookie, and _issued_cookie_names reads them all via get_all(), so taking only the head of each header is both correct and safe. Where a caller has already collapsed headers, it now under-reports rather than over-reports, which is the direction a redactor must fail in. Names are additionally validated against the RFC 6265 token charset.
defects_fixed.note: No leaked fragment reached the ledger: the 55 redacted values were single-cookie headers and all yielded one clean name.

defects_fixed.detail: request() caught only HTTPError, so a timeout, a reset connection or a body that died mid-read escaped before `calls += 1` and before _record. The module's own promise is that the ledger is complete by construction. Worse, contamination.py's sealed-pile audit defines contact as 'a sealed id in a request we sent' and can only see what the ledger holds -- so a call that genuinely went out on the wire carrying a sealed game_id and then timed out would have been invisible to the audit, and to the test asserting the audit is clean. That is the most load-bearing claim in the project resting on a check with a hole in it. Fixed: every request that leaves the process records exactly one row (status -1, transport_error set), increments the counter, and then re-raises so retry accounting is unchanged. Two tests, one of them the negative control showing the audit does catch a sealed id in a failed call.
defects_fixed.note: Pre-existing, not introduced by the cookie patch -- but the patch is what made the ledger the evidence base for the before/after, so it is fixed here.
defects_fixed.what: A failed request left no ledger row.

defects_fixed.detail: cookies_held was evaluated inside the _record call, which runs after HTTPCookieProcessor has already absorbed the response's Set-Cookie. So the log described the jar the call produced, not the jar that produced the call, and the first request of every session -- which provably sent no Cookie header -- was logged as though it held the server's cookies. Since HTTPCookieProcessor attaches the Cookie header inside open(), request_headers never showed it either, so 'did we echo them back' -- the INC-007 discriminator -- was unanswerable from the ledger for every line. Fixed: cookies_sent (snapshotted before the call) and cookies_held_after (the jar the response left).
defects_fixed.note: No published number depended on it: the 20/20 vs 0/20 and 8/8 results are counted from HTTP status codes.
defects_fixed.what: The cookie record was in the wrong tense.

defects_fixed.detail: It flagged a field only `if '=' in text`, but the name lists it checked are produced by split('=')[0] and by cookie.name, neither of which can contain '='. For two of its three fields the assertion was incapable of failing. Exactly the INC-003 shape, in the test written to prevent an INC-008 repeat. Fixed: names must match the cookie-token charset, and a positive control plants three value-shaped entries and asserts the detector finds all three.
defects_fixed.note: The detector did do real work on the raw set_cookie field, which is where the 55 offenders were.
defects_fixed.what: The value-detector test could not fail.

defects_fixed.detail: 40 identical retries worked because the jar-less transport re-drew a replica on every attempt. Once pinned, all 40 go to the same replica, so if that replica is the broken one, retrying is only waiting. Fixed: send_command drops the AWSALB* routing cookies every REDRAW_EVERY=5 failures, keeping GAMESESSION -- the session is the thing we are trying to reach, not the thing that is wrong. It almost never fires now (measured 1.00 attempt per command), but the envelope must not have silently regressed.
defects_fixed.note: Raised by the review as a wrong-measurement risk; it is really a robustness one, and is fixed rather than argued about.
defects_fixed.what: The pinned jar made the retry envelope weaker than what it replaced.

defects_fixed.detail: The ledger append wrote the record and its newline as two calls on a buffered stream while a second appender uses the same file, and 148 records exceed the 8 KiB buffer -- now one write. Redirects were followed but never recorded -- now final_url/redirected. The probe collapsed five Set-Cookie headers to one via dict(headers) and read the key case-sensitively -- now shares the client's reader. redact_ledger.py documented a --check flag argparse did not define. canary.py's baseline confirmation dropped the transport covariate the patch had just added, making http_calls a number without a unit.

detail: The INC-007a patch was put through a five-lens adversarial review (transport correctness, secret hygiene, regression blast radius, experiment soundness, record/code consistency) before the after-run's actions were spent. 30 findings were raised and 17 survived an independent refutation pass. The measured result of INC-007a is unaffected -- no published number changes -- but four defects were real and are fixed here, and one claim was overstated and is corrected.
evidence: arc-recon/test_hygiene.py (40 tests; 7 are regressions for the defects above, each with a negative control)
lesson: The review cost nothing that mattered and found a secret leak, a hole in the project's most load-bearing audit, and a test that could not fail. All three were in code written in the same session that was congratulating itself for catching INC-008. The general form: the instrument you just built to check something is the instrument nobody has checked.
title: Adversarial review of the cookie patch: the ledger could not evidence what it claimed, and the redactor leaked through itself
two_findings_were_stale: The review snapshotted the tree before INC-007a and INC-008 were filed, so its 'code cites INC-008 but no INC-008 exists' pair was already false when it landed. Verified against data/incidents.jsonl rather than taken on trust -- a reviewer's finding is a claim like any other.

an_own_goal_worth_recording: The first version of the new tests tried to redirect the probe log by monkeypatching ledger.PROBE_PATH. That does not work -- probe(kind, detail, path=PROBE_PATH) binds the default at definition time -- so two test entries were appended to the track's REAL, tracked, append-only probe_log.jsonl. Caught immediately, reverted with git checkout (the file was restored to its committed 1945 lines), and the tests now replace ledger.probe outright, which cannot write anywhere. A further test asserts the file's size does not move. Writing test noise into another track's append-only ledger would have been a small thing that is impossible to tidy later.
detail: The owner instructed this track to apply the cookie fix to baseline-arms' client as well. CLAUDE.md says 'Stay inside your own directory. Do not edit the other track's files', and P-11's own work order scopes this track to arc-recon/ with everything else read-only. The concern was stated and the instruction repeated, so it is carried out and recorded here rather than quietly. This entry exists so that the boundary crossing is visible to the track that owns those files.
evidence: arc-recon/data/incidents.jsonl INC-007a (the measurement this port relies on)
arc-recon/data/incidents.jsonl INC-009 (the three mistakes it avoids repeating)
merge_hazard: These files are P-12's territory (agent/p12-envelope-finish exists). If P-12 also edits arc_client.py or bare_cc.py, M-0 will see a conflict. The changes here are small and localised -- a constructor, a request body, two retry loops, one new test file -- so a conflict should be resolvable by hand, but it is a real cost of crossing the boundary and is flagged on PARTNER_SYNC rather than left to be discovered at merge.
title: Cross-track edit: the INC-007 cookie fix ported into baseline-arms/harness on owner instruction

verification.live_check: zero actions. One RESET on ar25-0c556536 through the patched client: HTTP 200 on the first attempt; the session's first call sent no cookies and every later call sent five; cookies_enabled true throughout; no value recorded anywhere; the sealed guard still refuses ls20 and ft09.
verification.their_suite: 32 passed (19 pre-existing whitelist tests unchanged, 13 new transport tests)
verification.why_ar25_and_not_g50t: g50t had two live processes on it. A RESET there could disturb a campaign seven hours into its run, and the check does not need it.
verification.why_no_writes_leaked: BASELINE_ARMS_SHARD=p11-verify routed the probe output to out/shards/, which is untracked -- using that track's own sharding mechanism rather than inventing one.

what_changed: baseline-arms/harness/arc_client.py -- one http.cookiejar.CookieJar per client through HTTPCookieProcessor, cookies=True by default and cookies=False retained so BUDGET_REPORT.md's figures can be reproduced; cookie NAMES only into the probe log, never values; cookies_sent captured before the call and cookies_held_after after it; final_url/redirected recorded; clear_routing_cookies().

baseline-arms/harness/bare_cc.py -- `resilient` and `reset_with_retry` drop the ALB pins every 5 failures (_redraw). D-005 sized those envelopes against a transport that re-drew a replica on every attempt; a pinned jar sends all 8 or all 30 retries to the same replica, so without this the fix would have made the envelope weaker than what it replaced.
baseline-arms/tests/test_transport.py -- new, 13 tests, each with a negative control.
what_this_does_not_do: No before/after measurement on baseline-arms' own workload. arc-recon's paired canary already establishes that the fix is behaviour-preserving and collapses amplification (190 -> 20 HTTP for 20 commands, identical frame hashes), and re-deriving it here would mean running their campaigns, which costs real money and real action quota and is that track's budget to spend. The consequence stands and is theirs to act on: every figure in BUDGET_REPORT.md carrying a 2.5-10x or 5.07x amplification term was measured on the jar-less transport and should be re-derived, not reinterpreted. cookies=False exists so the old regime can be reproduced side by side.
what_was_deliberately_not_changed: No file in the main checkout. The work was done in this branch's worktree, which is a separate copy on disk, because TWO PROCESSES WERE LIVE at the time: PID 37572 (harness.campaign --game g50t-5849a774, running since 02:42) and PID 14544 (harness.run --game g50t-5849a774 --model claude-opus-5, a first-contact run). Editing the files they import would not affect the running interpreters but would affect any process they spawn, and INC-BA-003 is precisely the incident about two sessions colliding in that directory.

None of baseline-arms' prose: DECISIONS.md, STATUS.md, BUDGET_REPORT.md and AUDIT.md are that track's narrative and remain theirs to write. The full rationale is in the module docstring, where a maintainer of that file will find it, and the change is announced on PARTNER_SYNC. They should record it as their own D-nnn.

an_arithmetic_note_to_prevent_confusion: `http_calls_gameplay` in the cell summary counts ACTION retries only; the decomposition counts every /api/cmd/ call, which also includes RESET retries (11 on the old arm, 1 on the new). 101 + 11 = 112 and 35 + 1 = 36; successes 14 + 1 = 15 and 18 + 1 = 19. The two views agree.
confounds_stated: One cell per arm. This is a demonstration in this track's units, not an estimate with an error bar.

Run back to back, not interleaved -- a whole cell cannot be interleaved. API conditions vary over minutes, and arc-recon measured 9.19 vs 11.88 http/action on two cookie-less canary sweeps 35 minutes apart, so treat single-cell differences under about 30% as noise.
Other processes were sharing the API and the account while this ran (INC-BA-003's standing hazard).
consequences_for_this_tracks_figures: BUDGET_REPORT.md's amplification terms (D-005's 5.07x, the 2.5-10x band) are confirmed as descriptions of the OLD transport and are now obsolete as forward estimates. Re-derive rather than reinterpret: the routing component is gone, the 500 component is not, and $/cell is not the quantity that moved. The G4 abort threshold (actions_failed >= 10) also needs revisiting -- the variance envelope's three cells all hit exactly 10 failures and were judged RED for degradation, but on this evidence that threshold was mostly measuring the transport, not the arm.

cost_of_this_measurement.note: two cells, cheapest model tier, budget 20 each; a cost ceiling of $2.00 per cell was set and not approached

detail: arc-recon's INC-007a measured the transport change on its own canary. This measures it where the money is actually spent: a real bare-CC cell, real model calls, real frames. Same game, same model, same budget, same code path -- the two runs differ only in ArcClient(cookies=...). Run back to back with the old transport first. harness/transport_ab.py; full record in baseline-arms/out/transport_ab.json; ledger and probe output went to an untracked shard (BASELINE_ARMS_SHARD=transport-ab) so neither of that track's append-only files moved.
evidence: baseline-arms/out/shards/probe_log.transport-ab.jsonl (untracked; every call with its status and cookie state)
not_done: The `resilient` retry policy was NOT changed to stop retrying deterministic 500s, although this run shows it is now the dominant waste. Changing it would alter the very retry accounting this A/B just measured, and it deserves its own before/after. Recommended as that track's next step.
One cell per arm. This is a demonstration in that track's units, not an estimate with an error bar.
g50t was avoided throughout: two live processes were on it.
read_the_dollars_carefully: Cost per cell went UP, $0.6480 -> $0.7064, and that is the fix working. A cell aborts at actions_failed >= 10; on the old transport an action fails when all eight retries miss, so cells died early with their money spent on retries rather than gameplay. The fixed cell survives to spend its whole budget. The figure that improves is cost per unit of actual gameplay: $0.0463 -> $0.0392 per successful action, with 14 -> 18 successful actions out of the same 20 commands and the same 20 model calls. Anyone quoting $/cell alone would report this fix as a regression.
the_before_arm_reproduces_the_historical: The M4 pilot's ar25 x haiku x budget-20 cell (out/pilot_ar25-0c556536.json, old transport) recorded 107 http / 20 commands = 5.35, 15 ok / 5 failed, 685s. This run's cookies=False arm: 5.05, 14 ok / 6 failed, 712s. Within noise of each other. That matters because it means the 'before' arm is a faithful reproduction of the regime every figure in BUDGET_REPORT.md was measured in, rather than a strawman -- and so the comparison carries over to those figures.

decomposition.the_next_bottleneck: `bare_cc.resilient` retries EVERY non-200 up to eight times, including 500s. On the old transport that was invisible: routing misses dominated. On the fixed transport 500s are most of what is left, and each one costs eight attempts to learn what the first attempt already said. arc-recon's precheck deliberately retries only `400 ... not found` / 429 / transport errors, on the grounds that burning a retry budget on a deterministic error is just a slower way of failing. Recommended next change for this track -- NOT made here, because it would alter the very retry accounting this A/B just measured, and it deserves its own before/after.
decomposition.verdict: Routing retries per successful gameplay call: 5.93 -> 0.05. That is the transport effect, isolated. The headline http_per_command ratio is SMALLER than this because the fixed arm's remaining traffic is almost entirely 500s being retried eight times each -- a different defect, described below.

the_headline_understates_it.headline: http per executed command 5.05 -> 1.75, a 2.89x improvement
the_headline_understates_it.what_the_residue_actually_is: Almost all of the fixed arm's remaining traffic is 500s: 16 of its 36 gameplay calls. `bare_cc.resilient` retries EVERY non-200 up to eight times, so each deterministic 500 costs eight attempts to learn what the first one already said. On the old transport this was invisible because routing misses dominated; removing the dominant failure promoted the next one.
the_headline_understates_it.why_that_is_too_modest: It lumps together two failures with opposite characters. A `400 game <id> not found` is the routing miss this whole exercise is about: the next attempt, from a different replica, succeeds. A `500` is the server refusing the request itself, and no number of retries changes its mind. Separated over gameplay calls only: **routing retries per successful call went 5.93 -> 0.05**, i.e. 89 routing misses became 1. That is the transport effect, isolated, and it is near-total.

title: The cookie fix measured on baseline-arms' own workload: one cell per transport, side by side
wall_clock_barely_moved: 712s -> 677s. A bare-CC cell is model-bound, not API-bound: 20 model calls dominate the clock, and the HTTP saved is a small share of it. The transport fix buys API efficiency and success rate, NOT wall clock. Any campaign schedule built on 'it will now run faster' is built on the wrong quantity.
